title: Infra Playbook: GPU Fleet, Cloud Accounts & IaC CI/CD (2026 Addendum)
author: Priya Singh
content:
Overview

This playbook is an operational reference for Redwood Inference infrastructure engineers responsible for the GPU fleet, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD pipelines, and on-call runbooks. It consolidates capacity planning, account hygiene, module guidance, and common operational procedures. It is an addendum to the core 2026 infra playbook and focuses on cross-cutting patterns and remediation steps encountered during fleet scale-up and multi-account networking rollouts.

Scope

- Audience: infra engineers, SRE, platform engineers, and solutions engineers supporting Dedicated and Private deployments.
- Systems covered: GPU fleet (K8s and bare-metal pools), cloud accounts (AWS/GC/azure onboarding patterns), VPC & networking, Terraform modules for fleet & cloud accounts, CI/CD build and release pipelines for infra modules, and runbooks for capacity incidents.
- Excluded: application-level model serving logic; model runtime tuning (see eng-serving-runtime docs).

Goals

1. Reduce incidents caused by capacity mis-sizing and misconfigured IAM/networking.
2. Standardize Terraform module patterns, testing, and releases.
3. Provide deterministic CI/CD and rollback procedures for infra changes.
4. Document runbook steps for the top 8 operational incidents impacting GPU pools.

Ownership and RACI

- Fleet capacity & autoscaler config: infra-capacity (primary), eng-sre (secondary)
- Cloud accounts, org structure, billing setup: cloud-accounts (primary), finance-legal (review)
- Terraform modules & module registry: infra-iac (primary), eng-developer-experience (docs)
- CI/CD pipelines for IaC: infra-ci (primary), eng-platform (support)

Key contacts

- Priya Singh (Infra Engineering) —  on-call lead for capacity runbooks
- Ethan Chen (SRE) —  autoscaler and monitoring owner
- Mariana Lopez (Cloud Accounts) — account bootstrap & billing
- Pager: #infra-oncall (Slack)

GPU Fleet & Capacity Planning

Principles

- Plan capacity for p95 load with 20% buffer during business hours.
- Separate pools by workload class: interactive-low-latency, batch-high-throughput, isolation-sensitive (customer-dedicated).
- Prefer vertical scaling (bigger instances) for latency-critical pools and horizontal scaling for batch pools.

Sizing checklist (pre-flight)

1. Collect 7-day token/sec distribution and peak concurrent sessions.
2. Run simulator (tools/capacity-sim) with service-level QPS and model seq_len histogram.
3. Calculate GPU count per pool: target_utilization = 65% for low-latency pools, 75% for batch pools.
4. Validate KV/cache hit rate and effective token reduction from prefix caching.

Capacity thresholds & SLOs

| Metric | Pool Type | Alert threshold | Action | Owner |
|---|---:|---:|---|---|
| GPU Utilization (avg 5m) | interactive | >75% | Prep scale-up (add nodes) | infra-capacity |
| Pending queue length | interactive | >10 | Increase replicas/priority preemption | eng-sre |
| Pod OOMs / failures | any | >=3 in 10m | Roll back recent changes; investigate memory config | infra-iac |
| Scheduling latency (p95) | batch | >30s | Adjust scheduler weights; increase nodes | infra-capacity |

Autoscaling guidance

- Use cluster-autoscaler with custom metrics exporter: gpu-utilization and pending-work-items. Tune scale-down cooldown to 15m for low-latency pools.
- For Dedicated pools with reserved capacity, prefer static node counts and soft alarms for burst policies.

Cloud Accounts & Networking

Account structure

- Use an organization-level hierarchy: org-root -> shared-services -> prod -> staging -> customer-dedicated (per-customer AWS accounts for Private).
- All accounts must be provisioned with the account bootstrap Terraform module (see Module Naming).

Networking patterns

- VPC-per-environment with standardized CIDR blocks (documented in configs/vpc-cidr-map.md).
- Transit Gateway or Shared-VPC for cross-account access; use explicit ACLs and route tables to limit blast radius.
- Egress policy: all outbound traffic from production must go through the egress proxy and be logged.

Security & IAM hygiene

- Least privilege by default; require role-based access via SSO groups and short-lived STS sessions.
- Use guardrails in Terraform: deny policies and Sentinel pre-commit checks in CI for public S3 buckets or broad IAM policies.

Terraform / IaC Modules & Patterns

Module naming & registry

- Prefix modules with ri- (example: ri-gpu-node-pool, ri-account-bootstrap, ri-vpc). Publish to private module registry with semantic versions.
- Maintain CHANGELOG.md per module and require at least one reviewer from infra-iac for major changes.

Module conventions

- Inputs: simple scalars or maps only. Avoid nested objects in public module interfaces.
- Outputs: explicit resource IDs and ARN strings.
- Version pinning: Consumers must pin module versions in root modules to avoid surprise changes.

Testing & QA

- Unit: terraform validate + tflint + checkov run on PR.
- Integration: module smoke tests in ephemeral accounts via infra-ci pipeline (plans applied to a disposable staging account).
- Policy: run policy engine (OPA/Sentinel) in CI gating step.

CI/CD and Build Pipelines

Pipeline roles

- Pull Request (PR) pipeline: terraform fmt, validate, tflint, checkov, plan. Requires human approval for apply to prod.
- Release pipeline: tags module versions, publishes to registry, and triggers downstream root module pipeline.

Canonical CI job examples (excerpt)

- PR job (infra-module-pr.yaml):
  - name: fmt-and-validate
    steps:
      - terraform fmt -check
      - terraform init -backend=false
      - terraform validate
      - tflint --config .tflint.hcl

- Release job (infra-module-release.yaml):
  - name: publish-module
    steps:
      - run: bump-version.sh && git tag -a v${NEW_VERSION} -m "release"
      - run: terraform publish --registry=private 

Promotions and rollbacks

- Promotion to prod requires: green CI, manual approval, and a one-hour maintenance window for modules that touch networking or account bootstrap resources.
- Rollback: revert module version in the consumer repo and apply in a controlled PR; use feature-flagged promos for complex changes.

Runbooks & On-call Procedures

Top incidents (with TL;DR run steps)

1. High scheduling latency causing request queueing (interactive pool)
   - Check: monitoring.grafana -> scheduler latency panel, cluster-autoscaler logs.
   - Immediate: increase pool replica count via ri-gpu-node-pool scale override; escalate to infra-capacity if scale does not stabilize in 10m.
   - Postmortem triggers: >15m degraded service or customer impact.

2. Sudden drop in available GPUs (node terminations)
   - Check: cloud provider events, auto-scaling group activity, kube node NotReady.
   - Immediate: verify autoscaler activity; replace nodes using the node replacement playbook (playbooks/node-replace.md).

3. Cross-account routing failure
   - Check: TGW route tables, security group changes, and VPC peering status.
   - Immediate: revert recent Terraform apply in shared-services and re-apply stable plan.

4. CI pipeline plan fails for prod apply
   - Check: plan diff, service account permissions.
   - Immediate: hold the apply, open a rollback PR for module change, and run plan in a disposable account for deeper diagnostics.

War Room checklist

- Add runbook link to incident Slack channel.
- Assign incident commander, owner, and scribe.
- Collect metrics: GPU utilization, scheduling latency, pending queue, and infra CI recent changes.

Upgrade and Rollout Guidance

- Rolling kernel or driver upgrades: drain nodes in small batches (5-10% of pool), validate no schedule regressions, check GPU-specific metrics (temperature, memory errors).
- Terraform major version upgrades: run a dry-run apply in a staging environment and maintain a migration plan with expected state diffs.

Appendix: Example Terraform module snippet

module "gpu_node_pool" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@repos.redwood/infra/ri-gpu-node-pool.git//modules/node-pool?ref=v1.4.0"
  name   = "interactive-usa-west-2"
  gpu_type = "nvidia-a100"
  min_nodes = 2
  max_nodes = 100
  labels = {
    pool = "interactive"
    env  = "prod"
  }
}

Appendix: Useful commands

- Check autoscaler status: kubectl get deployment cluster-autoscaler -n kube-system -o yaml | grep -i metrics
- Run planner locally: tools/capacity-sim --input telemetry/last-7d.json --pool interactive
- Create disposable account for module test: scripts/bootstrap-disposable-account.sh --env staging
